title: Paying in time
bodyMd:
When something popular is offered below the price people would willingly pay, it still has to be shared out somehow. Economists call this rationing, and one of its oldest forms is the queue. Imagine a town whose public swimming pool admits two hundred people on summer afternoons at a modest fixed fee. On hot days far more than two hundred want to swim, and the places go to those who arrive earliest and wait longest.

A queue is often described as the fair alternative to a price, because everyone has the same twenty-four hours in a day while not everyone has the same income. There is something to this. But a queue is not free; it is paid for in time rather than money, and the payment is simply destroyed. When a swimmer pays a higher fee, the pool receives the money and can spend it on lifeguards or longer opening hours. When a swimmer waits ninety minutes in the sun, nobody receives those ninety minutes.

Nor is time distributed as evenly as the slogan suggests. A retired person or a student on holiday can spare an afternoon more easily than a parent with a shift job, so the queue quietly favours those whose hours are least valuable to them, or least committed elsewhere. That may or may not match anyone's idea of who deserves to swim.

None of this means that the pool should simply raise its fee until the queue disappears. A price high enough to clear the line on the hottest days would exclude many families altogether, and the town may reasonably decide that a swim on a hot day is something it wants to offer regardless of income. The point is narrower. Choosing a queue is choosing a particular way of charging people, with its own winners and losers, and it should be weighed as such rather than treated as the absence of a charge. Some towns compromise: a share of the places is booked in advance at the ordinary fee, and the rest are left for those who turn up.
accessibilityText: A four-paragraph prose passage of about 340 words on queues as a way of rationing. The first paragraph introduces a hypothetical town pool that admits two hundred people at a modest fixed fee, with places on hot days going to those who arrive earliest and wait longest. The second paragraph grants that a queue is often called fair because everyone has the same hours in a day, but argues that waiting is a payment in time that nobody receives, unlike a fee that the pool can spend. The third paragraph argues that spare time is unevenly distributed, so the queue favours people such as retired people and students on holiday over a parent with a shift job. The fourth paragraph rejects simply raising the fee until the queue disappears, because that would exclude many families, and concludes that a queue is a particular way of charging people that should be weighed as such; it ends by mentioning that some towns book a share of places in advance at the ordinary fee.

provenance.notes: Original expository prose written for this question bank. The town and its pool are invented for illustration; no published article, essay or test passage was copied, paraphrased or reconstructed.
